title: I built a fully local text → 3D game asset pipeline on a single RTX 5090 [Open Source]
author: piddlefaffle12
selftext:
https://preview.redd.it/6mzhrppyl6ph1.png?width=2048&format=png&auto=webp&s=f0642e2511eb9113c648010da9f86d14c025c731

https://preview.redd.it/lqxkrrqzl6ph1.png?width=2048&format=png&auto=webp&s=de895484300958c28ec61f45950a64ff47788507

https://preview.redd.it/33wg6rc1m6ph1.png?width=2048&format=png&auto=webp&s=6a604614fdf78e0b2586deecc1e82e9debbf8655

**Type a prompt. About 11 minutes later, get a textured, optimized, game-ready 3D asset with LODs, collision, PBR textures, preview renders, and validation. All on one RTX 5090, fully local, with no hosted APIs.**

I spent the last day wiring together some of the best current open models and tools into a **fully local, agent-callable text → 3D game asset pipeline** running under Docker Desktop.

The goal was to see how close the current open-source stack can get to a practical "prompt in, usable game asset out" workflow without manually bouncing files between image generators, 3D models, Blender, and game engines.

You give it a prompt. It gives you:

* Textured high-quality master GLB
* Game-ready optimized mesh at a target triangle budget
* Baked PBR textures at a target resolution
* Multiple LODs
* Convex collision mesh
* Preview renders
* glTF + Godot validation
* A manifest containing every setting, measurement, warning, model revision, etc.

Nothing leaves the machine. No hosted APIs.

Repo: [https://github.com/zorrobyte/asset-studio](https://github.com/zorrobyte/asset-studio)

# The pipeline

**1. Prompt → structured asset prompt**

The input gets normalized into an asset template designed for image-to-3D generation: single object, plain background, three-quarter view, no text or logos, plus style presets such as *stylized mobile factory game*.

**2. Qwen-Image-2512 → reference image**

Runs through Diffusers in BF16 at full-quality 50 steps.

The transformer alone is about 41 GB, so because my Docker VM only has 46 GB of RAM, part of the model gets split between the 5090 and CPU RAM.

**3. Pixal3D → 3D master**

I'm using the newer TRELLIS.2-based Pixal3D pipeline with MoGe-2 camera estimation.

Typical output is roughly:

* \~1 million triangles
* PBR materials
* 4K textures

**4. Headless Blender → game asset**

Blender automatically handles:

* Scale/origin normalization
* Mesh cleanup
* Mesh optimization
* UV generation
* PBR texture baking
* LOD generation
* Convex collision
* Cycles preview renders

For reduction I'm using **meshoptimizer**, with error-bounded, attribute-aware simplification. It is basically the same simplifier used by gltfpack.

**5. Validation**

Every output is checked with:

* Khronos glTF Validator
* Headless Godot import

Then the entire run gets written into a manifest.

# Agent/API support

The whole thing runs behind FastAPI with durable SQLite jobs:

`POST /v1/jobs`

Then you can poll status, download artifacts, cancel jobs, retry them, or reprocess starting from a specific stage.

There's also:

* Dependency-free CLI
* Thin MCP wrapper
* Blender comparison viewer

So an AI coding agent can literally request something like:

>

...and receive a game-ready asset.

The comparison viewer opens the master, optimized mesh, LODs, and collision mesh side by side, both textured and untextured.

# Actual RTX 5090 numbers

These are measurements from my machine, not upstream H100 benchmarks:

|Stage|Time|Peak VRAM|
|:-|:-|:-|
|Qwen-Image 1328² / 50 steps|\~290 sec/image|\~27 to 31 GB|
|Pixal3D 1024|\~4 min|\~15 GB|
|Pixal3D 1536|\~3.7 min|\~25 GB|
|Blender + meshoptimizer|\~75 sec|CPU|

A normal "balanced" asset takes around **11 minutes end to end**.

Quality mode, where it generates two reference candidates first, is around **16 minutes**.

# Things I learned the hard way

**Pixal3D meshes are surprisingly difficult to optimize.**

The masters are usually around 1M triangles spread across something like 200 separate shells.

Blender's normal collapse decimate, and most quick simplifiers I tested, absolutely destroy thin geometry at game-ready triangle counts. Planks turn into holes, spikes appear, edges collapse, etc.

Using meshoptimizer with around a 5% error bound worked dramatically better.

If even that can't reach the requested budget cleanly, the pipeline voxel-remeshes a copy into a single shell first. That fallback gets explicitly recorded in the manifest as a warning.

A few other discoveries:

* The PyPI `meshoptimizer` wrapper is missing ctypes `argtypes` for `simplifyWithAttributes` and will segfault. I ended up binding the C function manually.
* NATTEN is required by Pixal3D's NAF upsampler. There are no wheels for Torch 2.11, but NATTEN 0.21.0 builds fine for `sm_120`.
* Don't ask image models to generate text or logos on the object. They still butcher it constantly.
* Pixal3D defaults to RMBG-2.0 for matting, which is gated. BiRefNet works as an open drop-in replacement.

Everything is pinned, including commits, model revisions, and container image digests, in a dependency manifest.

The repo also includes three actual sample outputs:

* Crate
* Pump station
* Mug with the handle opening preserved

Plus [`BENCHMARKS.md`](http://BENCHMARKS.md) with the measurements.

# Next

I'm working on a web UI next:

**prompt → image variations → pick candidates → 3D generation queue → asset library → download**

The bigger goal is to make this usable by coding and game-dev agents as an actual **local asset-generation backend**, rather than just another Gradio demo where a human has to manually move files between five different tools.

Have fun and if you improve it, please open a PR!

comments.author: kantorcodes1
comments.body: one thing I was curious about: `assetctl retry` POSTs a retry for any job id without checking the current job state first. if an agent retries a job that's still running, does the API reject it, restart that job in place, or queue another attempt? that lifecycle edge seems worth making explicit for agent callers.

replies.author: piddlefaffle12
replies.body: Good test case! I'll account for that

replies.author: piddlefaffle12
replies.body: And you were correct "Found the bug: retrying a running job doesn't error out properly, and the from\_stage retry deletes stage results before checking state, risking mid-run corruption. I'll fix both by having retry check state first and return 409 with a clear reason for running/queued/held jobs."

replies.author: kantorcodes1
replies.body: nice, that 409 state check fixes the retry edge. i work on HOL Guard, an open-source local check before agent-run commands execute. for `assetctl` i'd review `generate`, `retry`, and `cancel`; keep `status`, `list`, `capabilities`, and `health` automatic. that gives agents a stop before they start GPU work or change a running job. open to a small `assetctl` Guard extension?

comments.author: DaedalusRaistlin
comments.body:
Do you really need a 5090 though? I was able to do 1024 and 1536 resolution image to model on my 3060Ti using the 8Gb fork of Trellis2. 

The image generation I was not too happy with. I still just use Nanobanana for that via Google's API. It's a few cents per image that way. 

A few months ago I made a site that uses that API for 2d artwork. Last night I finally hooked Claude up to it, via an api it added, so now my games can generate 2D artwork place holders. 

I want to try doing something similar with Trellis2 next. My old pc now runs my 3060 Ti, so I could hand a lot of simple image to 3d generation to it. 

Still need to see if I get any different results on my new 5080. Surely double the ram and all the new tech should give it a higher resolution. But you seem to have the same resolution options as I did on my 3060 Ti, which feels odd. 

I'm fairly confident much of this could work on an 8Gb card too. 16Gb is the price sweet point for me. 32Gb is a pipe dream. 

Just think though - if all this fits in 8Gb or 16Gb, you might be able to run multiple generations at once, or activate higher resolution settings. I think you can get better results than you are right now.

replies.author: piddlefaffle12
replies.body: Static models only for now, just wanted something to point claude at to generate models for a mobile game. Was curious if I could get something working. Another user in the thread commented a 8gb image to 3d model!

replies.author: DaedalusRaistlin
replies.body: Yes, I did that :) There's a fork of Trellis2 that works on 8Gb cards. I did some tests on my 3060 Ti and was happy with low poly model generation. For high detail models it didn't really hold a candle to paid online models. But I'm wondering if your 32gb (I'm jealous) would allow higher detail.

comments.author: TemporalAgent7
comments.body:
Your industrial water pump is a perfect example of the kinds of issues I have with the trellis.2 (and hunyuan3d and similar models). It's a messy, squished, sloppy result.

I've been trying to go at it from the other direction and start with Blender, driven by qwen3.8:27b via mcp also locally running. If needed, I can spin up ComfyUI / Krea2 to generate textures.

The problem is the model is too simplistic and lacks detail. I actually don't think it's a llm provider issue because I tried using GPT-6 Astra, and the results are similarly lackluster.

However, doing it this way gives you very nice named meshes that you can animate in the game engine, or attach effects to, etc.

I wish there was a happy medium between the 2 approaches. I actually think starting with Blender first (or something like [Kiln](https://github.com/matthew-kissinger/kiln)) would yield better results long term, we just need to build a library of useful Python functions and tips / tricks / documentation specifically tailored at LLMs building game assets.

comments.author: ifyounasty99
comments.body:
The 1M tris / 200 shells part sounds painfully familiar. Once thin pieces start breaking during simplification, the “generation” step stops being the hard part and you end up spending most of the time fixing what came out.

Been thinking about the same setup from the other direction. If everything doesn’t have to stay local, Astra can call something like Meshy through API/MCP, pass the result into Blender, clean it there, then send it on to the engine.

You give up the fully local side, but there’s also less stuff to keep running and glued together yourself. Blender probably stays in the middle either way though. I still wouldn’t trust generated meshes to go straight into a game untouched.
